## Weekly highlights


## **Ocean rates –**[Freightos Baltic Index](https://app.terminal.freightos.com/fbx)


- **Asia-US West Coast** prices (FBX01 Weekly) decreased 6%.
- **Asia-US East Coast** prices (FBX03 Weekly) stayed level.
- **Asia-N. Europe** prices (FBX11 Weekly) decreased 1%.
- **Asia-Mediterranean** prices (FBX13 Weekly) increased 20%.


## **Air rates –**[Freightos Air Index](https://app.terminal.freightos.com/fax)


- **China – N. America** weekly prices decreased 9%.
- **China – N. Europe** weekly prices decreased 6%.
- **N. Europe – N. America** weekly prices increased 9%.


## **Analysis**


**Analysis**


Port operators and the ILWU Local 26 watchmen union arrived at a last-minute agreement Friday night[averting a labor disruption](https://www.joc.com/article/la-lb-maritime-employers-local-26-reach-tentative-deal-on-new-contract-6327510) at the ports of LA and Long Beach. The new agreement – which should be welcomed by the many shippers still working to move holiday inventories inland – remains tentative until ratification, but the union will continue working under its expired contract until it votes.


Last week’s Trump-Xi summit ended with[calls](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/china-halts-critical-minerals-ban-to-maintain-truce-with-us) for[stability](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-19/xi-says-he-s-committed-to-working-with-trump-as-two-leaders-meet) in the trade relationship, and China has taken additional[conciliatory steps](https://www.wsj.com/economy/trade/china-to-suspend-some-critical-material-export-curbs-to-u-s-until-january-35bc8dca) since then. Nonetheless, the sides are[preparing options](https://mykn.kuehne-nagel.com/news/article/china-sharpens-legal-arsenal-for-return-of-us) should they become necessary, as the January 10th truce expiration approaches.


The USTR may[release the findings of its Section 301 investigations](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/us-readies-tariff-hike-on-china-eu-goods-as-soon-as-tuesday) into excess manufacturing capacity practices by a list of countries including China as early as next week. Several of the countries targeted by the study have[rejected the accusations](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/handful-g20-countries-reject-us-stance-excess-industrial-capacity-2026-10-02/) . But as these new tariffs would likely only[restore duties to IEEPA levels](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/new-trump-tariffs-won-t-top-trade-deal-levels-will-be-targeted) – which were agreed upon by the US and those trade partners last year – it is unclear whether or not some countries will view these steps as escalations and take retaliatory measures as a result.


Even if findings are released soon however, the[typical procedural next steps](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-121/t19/s2414/#:~:text=shall%20provide%20an%20opportunity) – a comments period followed by hearings – would likely mean a couple more months until the president could actually introduce tariffs based on the report. President Trump only enacted tariffs based on the most recent 301 investigation, which focused on issues of forced labor,[eight weeks after the USTR released](https://ustr.gov/trade-topics/enforcement/section-301-investigations/section-301-failure-impose-and-effectively-enforce-prohibition-importation-goods-produced-forced) its report.


Expectations of tariff increases may be among[the several converging drivers](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/frothy-transpacific-barrels-new-year-peter-tirschwell-crbcc/) of stronger than anticipated transpacific container volumes and the extended peak season over the last few months. Weather-driven congestion and capacity reductions may also have helped keep container rates higher for longer even as demand has cooled.


But transpacific spot prices have finally started to ease on these lanes. Asia – N. America West Coast rates fell 6% to about $8,000/FEU last week, with daily rates so far this week down to $7,500/FEU, their lowest level since the end of August. East Coast prices were stable at $9,800/FEU but have slid to $9,000/FEU and back to July levels so far this week. But rates are still nearly three times higher than a year ago.


Carriers are[increasing blanked sailings](https://theloadstar.com/transpac-spots-finally-on-the-slide-but-asia-med-spike-a-surprise/) as volumes cool, and with only a few weeks until pre-Lunar New Year demand kicks in, prices are still likely to be quite elevated when they start climbing again.


Despite the post-peak, pre-LNY volume lull on Asia – Europe lanes, carrier GRIs are pushing rates up – at least for now. Asia – N. Europe prices dipped 1% last week but have climbed about $200/FEU so far this week to $3,500/FEU. Mediterranean rates spiked 20% to about $5,200/FEU last week and daily rates have so far increased another $300/FEU, though current market dynamics do make it possible that prices will backslide in the near term.


When LNY demand does pick up though, some forwarders[expect existing congestion in N. Europe](https://www.joc.com/article/asia-europe-pre-lunar-new-year-peak-hits-amid-poor-reliability-port-congestion-6326542) to worsen, which will help put upward pressure on rates and could lead carriers to start rolling some contracted volumes again.


In air cargo,[seasonal demand is stacking on top of](https://theloadstar.com/korean-air-maximises-americas-capacity-as-ai-cargo-adds-to-peak-pressure/) the surge in shipments needed for data center construction on some Far East – N. America lanes to push rates up with only about three weeks of peak season to go.


Freightos Air Index South East Asia – N. America prices have climbed 15% to about $8.00/kg over the past month marking a 50% gain compared to last year. Far East – N. America rates cooled 9% last week to $8.40/kg with daily prices showing a further correction, possibly reflecting capacity additions as demand increases. China – Europe prices dipped 6% to $4.74/kg last week. This rate is just a 15% premium to last year as[the lane is still adjusting](https://theloadstar.com/black-friday-bundles-test-retail-margins-as-eu-parcel-charges-bite/) to the sharp drop in e-commerce volumes since EU changes to de minimis this summer.


Transatlantic rates climbed another 9% to an average of $3.56/kg last week and to its highest since June 2022. Europe-US peak season demand is likely combining with Asia-origin volumes seeking alternative routes to the US as long-haul space tightens. Winter schedules and freighter shifts to higher volume lanes may also be adding upward pressure on rates.
